hints: Think about what volatility means in terms of boiling point, and recall the states of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature.
Identify which intermolecular force acts between non-polar halogen molecules and how electron number changes from chlorine to iodine.
walkthrough:
Translate volatility into boiling**
Picture the halogens at room temperature. Chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid. That tells you boiling point increases down the group, so it gets harder to vaporise. In other words, volatility decreases.

Focus on what holds molecules together**
Halogens are simple covalent molecules like $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and $\text{I}_{2}$. When they boil you do not break the strong covalent bond inside the molecule. You only overcome the weak attractions between molecules, which are London dispersion (induced dipole-dipole) forces.

Link more electrons to stronger forces**
From $\text{Cl}_{2}$ to $\text{I}_{2}$ the number of electrons increases greatly. The larger electron cloud is more easily distorted to form temporary dipoles, so the London dispersion forces get stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

Final answer: Volatility decreases from chlorine to iodine.
Down the group there are more electrons per molecule so stronger London dispersion (induced dipole-dipole) forces between molecules.

hints: Thermal decomposition of $\text{HX}$ requires breaking the $\text{H-X}$ bond, so think about how $\text{H-Cl}$, $\text{H-Br}$ and $\text{H-I}$ bond strengths compare.
walkthrough:
Connect stability to bond breaking**
Thermal stability means resistance to breaking apart on heating. For $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$, decomposition involves breaking the $\text{H-X}$ bond. The weaker that bond, the less heat is needed.

Recall why H-I is weakest**
Iodine is the largest halogen atom, so the $\text{H-I}$ bond is longest with poorest orbital overlap. It has the lowest bond enthalpy of the three, so $\text{HI}$ decomposes most readily and is least thermally stable.
Final answer: $\text{HI}$ has the lowest $\text{H-X}$ bond enthalpy, so the $\text{H-I}$ bond is broken most easily on heating.

hints: Use the electronegativity table to work out the polarity of the $\text{H-F}$ bond compared with the $\text{H-I}$ bond.
Recall the special intermolecular force that only very electronegative atoms like F bonded to H can set up, and compare it with the forces between $\text{HI}$ molecules.
walkthrough:
Compare bond polarity from the data**
Fluorine is 4.0 and hydrogen is 2.1, a very large difference, so $\text{H-F}$ is very polar. Iodine is 2.5, very close to hydrogen at 2.1, so $\text{H-I}$ is only very slightly polar.

Assign the correct intermolecular forces**
$\text{HF}$ can form hydrogen bonds, the strongest type of permanent dipole-dipole attraction, because F is small and highly electronegative and bonded to H. $\text{HI}$ cannot form hydrogen bonds and relies essentially on weak instantaneous dipole induced dipole (London dispersion) forces.

Link force strength to boiling point**
Hydrogen bonds between $\text{HF}$ molecules are much stronger than the London forces between $\text{HI}$ molecules. More thermal energy is needed to overcome the attractions in $\text{HF}$, so $\text{HI}$ has the lower boiling point.

Final answer: $\text{HF}$ has hydrogen bonding / strong permanent dipole-dipole forces whereas $\text{HI}$ has only instantaneous dipole induced dipole (London dispersion) forces.
Intermolecular forces in $\text{HI}$ are weaker than those in $\text{HF}$, so less energy is needed to separate $\text{HI}$ molecules.

hints: Recall the equation for chlorine with hot concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ giving $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{NaClO}_{3}$ and water, then replace Cl with I in the same molar ratio.
walkthrough:
Use the chlorine pattern**
You know chlorine disproportionates with hot concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ to give chloride and chlorate(V): $3\text{Cl}_{2} + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_{3} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Iodine reacts in the same way.

Write the iodine analogue**
Simply swap every Cl for I. Iodine is simultaneously reduced to $\text{I}^{-}$ in $\text{NaI}$ and oxidised to $\text{IO}_{3}^{-}$ in $\text{NaIO}_{3}$. Balancing already matches: $$3\text{I}_{2} + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaI} + \text{NaIO}_{3} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Think of the reagent used to replace $\text{-OH}$ by $\text{-Br}$ or $\text{-I}$, made from red phosphorus and the halogen.
walkthrough:
Recognise the transformation**
You are swapping $\text{-OH}$ in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ for $\text{-I}$ to make $\text{CH}_{3}\text{I}$. This is nucleophilic substitution by iodide.

Choose the iodide source**
Concentrated $\text{HI(g)}$ works, or phosphorus triiodide $\text{PI}_{3}$ generated from red phosphorus and iodine. Both supply $\text{I}^{-}$ to replace the $\text{OH}$ group.
Final answer: $\text{HI(g)}$ or $\text{PI}_{3}$ (made from P and $\text{I}_{2}$).

hints: Ethene has a $\text{C=C}$ double bond attacked by an electrophile, so recall the standard two word name for addition of halogens to alkenes.
walkthrough:
Spot the alkene reaction type**
Ethene $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CH}_{2}$ plus $\text{I}_{2}$ gives $\text{CH}_{2}\text{ICH}_{2}\text{I}$. Two atoms add across the double bond with no other product, so it is addition.

Add the electrophile detail**
The $\text{C=C}$ pi bond is electron rich and is attacked first by the electrophilic end of $\text{I}_{2}$. The full name is therefore electrophilic addition.
Final answer: Electrophilic addition.

hints: Find the longest carbon chain containing the C bonded to I, number to give the iodine the lowest number, and name the methyl branch on the same carbon.
walkthrough:
Read the skeleton**
The diagram shows a central C bonded to I, to two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups and to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. The longest chain through that carbon is 4 carbons, so the parent is butane.

Number and name**
Number from the end nearest the I bearing carbon to give position 2. There is an iodine and a methyl group both on C2, giving 2-iodo-2-methylbutane.

hints: $\text{I}$ is replaced by $\text{OH}$ using aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, so decide whether $\text{OH}^{-}$ acts as a nucleophile or a base here.
walkthrough:
Compare J and K**
J is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C(I)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and K is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. Only $\text{I}$ has been replaced by $\text{OH}$.

Link conditions to mechanism**
Aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ provides $\text{OH}^{-}$ acting as a nucleophile to substitute $\text{I}^{-}$. This is nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis of a tertiary iodoalkane).
Final answer: Nucleophilic substitution.

hints: Ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ removes $\text{HI}$ from adjacent carbons, and L already uses H from the $\text{CH}_{2}$ next to C2, so think where else H can be removed.
walkthrough:
See elimination choices**
J is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C(I)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. Ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ causes elimination of $\text{HI}$. Removing H from C3 gives L, 2-methylbut-2-ene $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_{3}$.

Draw the other alkene**
Removing H from one of the two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups on C2 gives the terminal alkene: $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, which is 2-methylbut-1-ene. That is structure M.
Final answer: M is 2-methylbut-1-ene, $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$.

hints: For geometrical isomerism each C of the $\text{C=C}$ must carry two different groups, so look closely at the two groups on the left hand C of L.
walkthrough:
Apply the test for geometrical isomerism**
You need two different groups on each carbon of the double bond. Look at L, $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_{3}$.

Spot the repeated group**
The left carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ carries two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups which are identical. Swapping them gives the same structure, so no cis and trans forms exist.
Final answer: L has two identical methyl groups on one carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ bond, so cis-trans isomerism is not possible.

hints: Hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ in L, and the $=\text{CHCH}_{3}$ fragment with one H is oxidised further than an aldehyde.
walkthrough:
Split L at the double bond**
L is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_{3}$. Cleavage gives a $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}=$ fragment and a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}=$ fragment.

Assign oxidation products**
The $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}=$ part with no H gives propanone $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}=\text{O}$. The $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}=$ part with one H is oxidised fully to a carboxylic acid, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$, ethanoic acid.
Final answer: Ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$.

hints: This is the iodoform test on a methyl ketone, so the carbon fragment products are ethanoate and triiodomethane.
Balance I then O and H using $\text{OH}^{-}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, remembering the given $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{3}$ needs 3 $\text{I}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Recognise the iodoform reaction**
Propanone $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{3}$ contains $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-$ and reacts with excess alkaline iodine to cleave one methyl group as triiodomethane $\text{CHI}_{3}$, leaving ethanoate $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$.

Complete and balance**
Three $\text{I}_{2}$ molecules supply the three I atoms for $\text{CHI}_{3}$ plus three $\text{I}^{-}$ ions. Balancing O, H and charge with $\text{OH}^{-}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ gives: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{3} + 3\text{I}_{2} + 4\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O} + 3\text{I}^{-} + \text{CHI}_{3}$$

hints: Recall the characteristic colour and state of the $\text{CHI}_{3}$ solid formed in a positive iodoform test.
walkthrough:
Recall the visual test**
The iodoform reaction is used as a test because $\text{CHI}_{3}$ is very distinctive. It appears as a pale yellow solid that comes out of solution, so you observe a yellow precipitate.
Final answer: Yellow precipitate (yellow solid).
